FOR campaign/the-granary — SAME TEST, SECOND ASSERTION. main untouched at efb2ab304, 133.7s.

    domesday::anomaly::tests::evaluable_columns_measured_surface_on_the_226_column_census
      assertion failed: excluded count moved — re-measure and update this
        left: 50   right: 51

YOUR FIX WAS CORRECT AND INCOMPLETE, and the incompleteness is structural rather than careless. That test has TWO sequential pins:

    assert_eq!(evaluable.len(), 117, ...)   <- you fixed this, 114 -> 117
    assert_eq!(excluded.len(),   51, ...)   <- this one, needs 51 -> 50

`assert_eq!` panics, so the first failure ABORTS the test before the second ever runs. While `evaluable` was wrong you could not see that `excluded` was also wrong. Fix them one at a time and you pay one full chamber run per assertion — this is your second, and there are no more in that test, so the next one should clear it.

BOTH VALUES FOR A 229-COLUMN CENSUS: evaluable 117, excluded 50. That is 167 of 229 accounted for; the remainder are the columns the surface does not classify either way.

THIS IS A KNOWN SHAPE AND IT IS WORTH THE MINUTE IT TAKES TO GENERALISE. An earlier campaign in this repo shipped a guard wrong twice for exactly this reason, both times green, both found only by mutating the source: when assertions are sequential, an earlier one masks every later one, so a green tells you only that the FIRST assertion passes. The repo's own habit is to mutate assertions separately for that reason. Applied here: when a test carries several `re-measure and update this` pins against one derived quantity, re-measure ALL of them in one pass rather than chasing the reported one — the reporter can only ever name the first.

If you would rather not pay another round trip on a third hidden pin, the cheap local check is to run that one test after fixing, which costs seconds:

    cargo nextest run -p hornvale-lab -E 'test(evaluable_columns_measured_surface)'

MY OWN NOTE: I did not pre-screen this run, deliberately — last round I screened two known failures, saw green, and a third failed, so I said I would either screen the whole gate or none. That decision stands and it did not help you here. I could have run that single test in seconds and caught the second assertion before spending 274s of box time. "Whole gate or none" was the wrong rule; the right one is that a screen is worth running when it targets the thing that just failed, and worthless when it targets a set I chose from memory.

Box is free, nothing queued.
